news.author: Andrea Unger
news.content:
When discussing the stock market, most people tend to focus on what happens during regular Wall Street trading hours. After all, that is when most trading takes place.

Yet one often overlooked aspect is that prices can also change between one session’s close and the next session’s open. How much do these moves actually contribute to overall returns?

In this article, we will explore that question by comparing the historical performance of the regular trading session, also known as the cash session, with overnight performance in SPY, the ETF that tracks the S&P 500 Index. We will then break down overnight results by day of the week and examine how profits and drawdowns change when we limit trading to Monday, Tuesday, and Wednesday nights.

Why Use the SPY ETF to Analyze the S&P 500?

For our analysis, we will use SPY, one of the world’s most liquid ETFs. Because it tracks the S&P 500 Index, it provides a useful reference for studying the behavior of the U.S. stock market.

We chose this instrument for a reason. Rather than using instruments commonly employed in systematic trading, such as S&P 500 futures, we are focusing on an ETF, which has a simpler structure and does not require us to manage contract expirations. Futures are more complex instruments, and rolling from one contract to the next can introduce price discontinuities known as rollover gaps. If not handled properly, these gaps can distort the results of the analysis.

The goal of this article is less about developing a trading system ready for live trading and more about analyzing market behavior and identifying potential recurring patterns.

Each trader can then assess whether and how to capitalize on any edge identified in the analysis, choosing the instrument that best suits their needs while considering factors such as accessibility, trading costs, and capital efficiency.

Cash vs. Overnight Sessions: Comparing Returns in SPY

Let’s begin with Figure 1, which compares the performance of two strategies: one that trades exclusively during the cash session and another that holds positions only overnight.

By cash session, we mean the period from 9:30 a.m. to 4:00 p.m. Eastern Time. The strategy buys $10,000 worth of SPY at the market open and closes the position at the end of the same session, holding no position overnight.

The overnight session, by contrast, runs from one trading session’s close to the next session’s open. In this case, the strategy buys SPY at 4:00 p.m. and sells it at 9:30 a.m. on the next trading day, capturing price changes between the two sessions, including any opening gaps.

Figure 1. Comparison of cash-session and overnight trading results in the SPY ETF.

At first glance, the results appear clear: the overnight session substantially outperformed the cash session, generating a total profit of approximately $15,000, compared with roughly $5,900 during regular trading hours.

A closer look at the two curves, however, reveals two quite different periods.

Before 2010, the gap between the two equity curves gradually widened. In other words, while the overnight session contributed positively to market gains, the cash session delivered much weaker results, at times accumulating substantial losses.

From 2010 onward, that difference appears less pronounced. Both sessions contributed positively to stock market gains, and the cash session performed considerably better than it had during the previous decade. Another interesting observation emerges during two specific downturns: the pandemic-related crash in 2020 and the market decline in 2022. In both cases, the cash session held up relatively better than the overnight component, which experienced sharper declines.

Based on the overall results, however, the overnight session offers the more promising starting point for further analysis. Let’s focus exclusively on this component and examine how its returns are distributed across the days of the week.

The goal is to determine whether the observed edge is spread evenly across the week or tends to be concentrated on particular days.

Overnight Trading in SPY: Results by Day of the Week

In Figure 2, we have broken down the overnight strategy’s results by day of the week, producing five separate equity curves.

The strategy works as described above, except that each curve includes only trades initiated on a specific day. For example, the Monday curve shows the results of buying SPY at Monday’s close and selling it at Tuesday’s open. Similarly, the Friday curve includes trades opened at Friday’s close and closed at the following Monday’s open, covering the weekend as well.

The results reveal clear differences across the days of the week. Monday’s overnight session stands out as the most profitable historically, generating a total profit of more than $7,300, well above the results for any other day.

The Tuesday, Wednesday, and Friday overnight sessions also produced positive overall results, although their profits were considerably smaller, at approximately $3,400, $2,500, and $2,700, respectively.

Thursday is the clear exception: it is the only day of the week with a negative overall result, recording a loss of approximately $900.

These results show that the edge observed in the overnight session is not evenly distributed throughout the week but varies by day.

At this point, a natural question arises: what would happen if we traded only on the days that delivered the most promising results?

For example, we could limit trading to the Monday, Tuesday, and Wednesday overnight sessions. We would exclude Thursday because of its negative results, and Friday, despite its positive performance, to avoid the additional risks associated with holding a position over the weekend.

Figure 2. Cumulative results of the overnight strategy in SPY, broken down by day of the week.

Monday Through Wednesday Overnight Trading: Effects on Profits and Drawdowns

In Figure 3, we compare the original overnight strategy with a more selective version that trades only on Monday, Tuesday, and Wednesday nights, excluding the Thursday and Friday sessions.

The results are particularly interesting. Despite taking fewer trades, the modified strategy retains most of the original strategy’s total profit, with approximately $13,300 versus $15,000.

The most significant improvement, however, concerns risk. Looking at the two equity curves, we can see that the more selective version follows a much smoother path, with substantially smaller drawdowns.

This is reflected in the ratio of net profit to maximum drawdown, which rises from 3.7 for the original strategy to 9.6 for the modified version, more than two and a half times the original value.

In other words, trading less frequently allows us to achieve nearly the same profit with considerably less risk exposure. This result highlights the importance of identifying a statistical edge and understanding when to put it to work.

Figure 3. Comparison of the overnight strategy in SPY without a day-of-week filter and the version with entries limited to Monday through Wednesday.

The Overnight Risk Premium: One Possible Explanation for the Results

Our analysis shows that a substantial share of historical U.S. stock market returns has occurred during the overnight session, with marked differences across the days of the week.

But why does this happen? One possible explanation is the so-called overnight risk premium. Investors who hold positions overnight remain exposed to economic news, geopolitical events, and potential opening gaps, without always being able to respond promptly. The positive returns observed could therefore represent compensation for taking on this additional risk.

If that were the main explanation, however, we might also expect particularly strong results from the Friday overnight session, which spans the entire weekend and involves longer exposure to unexpected events. Instead, although this session was profitable, its performance fell well short of the Monday overnight session.

The risk premium therefore remains one possible interpretation, but it is unlikely to explain all the differences observed, particularly those between individual days of the week.

What we can say, however, is that simply filtering trades by day of the week preserved most of the historical profits while significantly reducing drawdown.

Once again, we have seen how even a straightforward analysis of market behavior can provide a useful starting point for identifying new systematic trading opportunities.

Until next time, happy trading!

Wall Street rallied Wednesday after Democrats won control of both chambers of Congress in Tuesday’s midterm elections, putting the Dow Jones Industrial Average on course for its biggest one-day gain in 19 months.

Oil tumbled on bets the result will push Washington toward an end to the Iran war. West Texas Intermediate crude fell 7.2% to $89.17 a barrel, and Brent sank 8.5% to $94.84.

Iran’s parliament speaker, Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, wrote on X that American voters “said NO TO WAR, and we endorse this message,” while President Donald Trump told the Financial Times the U.S. is “locked and loaded if we need to go, but there may be no reason for it.”

  • The S&P 500 rose 1.8% to 7,701, up 133 points.
  • The Dow gained 1,515 points, or 2.9%, to 53,302, its largest one-day advance in both points and percentage terms since April 9, 2025.
  • The Nasdaq 100 rose 1.3% to 28,557.
  • The Russell 2000 advanced 1.5% to 2,856
  • The CBOE Volatility Index dropped 16.7% to 17.35.
  • Bonds also rallied: The 10-year Treasury yield fell 6 basis points to 4.90%. The 2-year yield slipped 5 basis points to 4.58%, and the 30-year yield dropped 4 basis points to 5.30%.
  • Gold rose 3.3% to $4,070 an ounce and silver jumped 4.9% to $52.20.
  • Bitcoin (CRYPTO: BTC) climbed 4% to $80,432, back above $80,000.

On the data front, the ISM services PMI eased to 54.5 in October from 54.9, below the 54.8 forecast, while the prices-paid gauge cooled to 73 from 74. ADP private payrolls rose by 86,000, above the 69,000 forecast.

The Energy Select Sector SPDR Fund (NYSE:XLE) was the laggard, down 5.4% as crude slid, with the SPDR S&P Oil & Gas Exploration & Production ETF (NYSE:XOP) off 6.9%.

Advanced Micro Devices Inc. (NASDAQ:AMD) is taking on billions of dollars in potential financial obligations to help customers build AI data centers, as it steps up its challenge to Nvidia Corp. (NASDAQ:NVDA).

AMD’s lease guarantees jumped 88% in just three months, from $4.1 billion in June to $7.7 billion in September. Another $750 million in debt guarantees brings the total potential exposure to approximately $8.5 billion.

If its partners run into financial trouble, AMD could be on the hook for as much as $8.5 billion.

AMD has also signed another $13.3 billion in data-center leases that haven’t started yet. It plans to pass the facilities on to partners, but could still be left paying the rent if those partners can’t.

Why AMD Is Backing Data Centers

AMD is helping customers secure data centers where its chips can be installed, potentially generating billions in future sales.

On Tuesday’s earnings call, Bank of America analyst Vivek Arya questioned whether customers had sufficient financing, land and power to support roughly 3 gigawatts of planned AMD deployments in 2027.

CEO Lisa Su said AMD was working closely with customers to prepare infrastructure years in advance.

“We know where the GPUs are going in terms of which data centers and which locations,” Su said, adding that AMD was being “selective and strategic” about investing alongside partners.

A July deal with Core Scientific Inc. (NASDAQ:CORZ) shows how AMD is helping create a market for its own chips.

Core Scientific agreed to provide data-center capacity for 529 megawatts of computing. AMD leased 377 megawatts itself and provided financial backing for a cloud provider taking the remaining 152 megawatts.

That helps secure the facilities where AMD’s processors can be deployed, but also leaves the chipmaker exposed if its partners cannot pay.

And there’s a potential reward beyond chip sales. AMD received warrants to buy up to 30 million Core Scientific shares at $23.47 each, with its rights increasing as more capacity is leased.

Nvidia Is Playing the Same Game

Nvidia is pursuing a similar strategy on a much larger scale.

Its August filing revealed $108.5 billion in potential guarantees, including $105 billion backing a massive Ohio data center leased to OpenAI.

In return, the 4.25-gigawatt campus will use Nvidia’s AI hardware almost exclusively. Nvidia estimates each generation of equipment installed there could generate $150 billion to $200 billion in revenue.

The guarantees take effect in stages starting in fiscal 2029, with payments required only if OpenAI defaults.

No Defaults So Far

AMD ended September with $15.8 billion in cash and short-term investments. No commercial partners had defaulted, and AMD had made no guarantee payments.

But the chipmaker warned that financing problems, permitting delays or partners failing to meet their obligations could force it to make payments “without realizing the anticipated economic benefits.”

news.author: Chandrima Sanyal
news.content:
The Democratic takeover of Congress sparked a powerful rally across Wall Street on Wednesday, lifting broad-market ETFs such as the Vanguard Total Stock Market ETF (NYSE:VTI) and the State Street SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust (NYSE:SPY). However, diverging moves among mega-cap technology stocks, semiconductor companies and AI infrastructure plays suggest the rally is not as broad-based as it appears.

VTI was up about 1.7% Wednesday. The advance came as the Dow Jones Industrial Average surged more than 3%. The S&P 500 was up 1.8%, while the Nasdaq Composite had gained about 1.8%.

The rally followed Democratic victories in both chambers of Congress, with investors betting that greater political gridlock could limit sweeping policy changes and reduce uncertainty around the economic outlook.

Mega-Cap Technology Stocks Drive the Rally

The biggest contributors to Wednesday’s advance included some of Wall Street’s largest technology companies, although gains were far from universal.

Apple Inc. (NASDAQ:AAPL) surged approximately 6% to a record high, while Microsoft Corp. (NASDAQ:MSFT) also climbed around 6%. Amazon.com Inc. (NASDAQ:AMZN) advanced about 7%, providing a significant boost to large-cap equity exposure.

However, Nvidia Corp. (NASDAQ:NVDA), VTI’s largest holding, fell about 1.5%. Tesla Inc. (NASDAQ:TSLA), another major holding, declined more than 2%.

The divergence matters because VTI, despite tracking nearly the entire U.S. stock market, remains heavily influenced by its largest constituents. Its top 10 holdings account for approximately 35% of the portfolio, according to Yahoo Finance data.

SPY has a similar exposure to mega-cap technology companies, as its S&P 500 benchmark is dominated by America’s largest publicly traded businesses. Consequently, both ETFs are benefiting from strength in Apple, Microsoft and Amazon while facing some headwinds from weakness in semiconductor stocks.

The Catch: A Rally With Uneven Participation

The weakness in semiconductor and AI infrastructure stocks highlights the underlying tension in Wednesday’s market rally.

Investors are weighing the possibility that Democratic control of Congress could bring greater scrutiny of AI development and data center construction. Democrats made significant gains in key data-center states, including Texas, raising concerns about tighter local regulations and potential delays to infrastructure projects.

Semiconductor stocks and data-center operators came under pressure even as major technology companies rallied. The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index fell more than 4% at one point, while some data-center operators suffered much steeper losses.

This creates a mixed backdrop for VTI and SPY, both of which have meaningful exposure to companies tied to the AI investment cycle.

VTI or SPY: What Should Investors Watch?

The key question is whether the post-election rally will broaden beyond mega-cap technology stocks.

If gains remain concentrated among the largest companies, SPY’s exposure to the S&P 500 could remain advantageous. However, if smaller companies and other market segments begin participating more meaningfully, VTI could benefit from its broader market coverage.

For now, Wednesday’s trading suggests that investors are rewarding select mega-cap technology companies while reassessing the outlook for semiconductor and AI infrastructure stocks.

President Donald Trump took to Truth Social on Wednesday to declare the "Stock Market just hit another Record High," less than a day after Democrats swept the House and the Senate in Tuesday’s midterm election.

“Stock Market just hit another Record High — 91 Days in just a short period of time — Less than two years. Your 401(k)s are through the roof. Record Setting All! President DONALD J. TRUMP,” he wrote.

The Dow Jones, tracked by the State Street SPDR Dow Jones Industrial Average ETF (NYSE:DIA) rallied 1,500 points and headed for its best day in 18 months as the decisive Democratic victory, along with Trump’s acceptance of the results, removed political uncertainty hanging over Wall Street.

None of the major indexes hit a record, though.

The Dow came closest in point terms but still fell well short. Its intraday high was 53,370.64, while its 52-week range tops out at 54,744.33, which leaves Wednesday’s peak roughly 2.5% below the record.

The Invesco QQQ Trust (NASDAQ:QQQ), which tracks the Nasdaq-100, peaked at a day high of $701.45 on Wednesday, about 8% below its 52-week high of $762.86, set on Oct. 6.

Trump Media & Technology Group Corp. (NASDAQ:DJT) shares were down 24.2% at $4.51 as of 3:30 p.m. ET Wednesday, a new 52-week low, according to Benzinga Pro market data

Democrats’ Sweep Lifts Dow 2.9% and Knocks Oil 7%

Trump’s post followed a sharp political shift. A Wednesday report said Democrats’ sweep of Congress lifted hyperscalers and retailers, while sinking oil and data-center builders and pulling yields lower. The Dow rallied 2.9% and oil prices fell by 7% after the midterms.

Trump Links 401(k) Gains to Investor Optimism After Midterms

Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas) said Wednesday that high prices cost Republicans control of Congress and warned that the economy could tip into recession if Democrats shut down planned projects.

Strong Markets Hide the Pain

In a post on X, Cruz said that Republicans leaned on macro numbers showing soaring stock markets, record median income and record-low poverty, but those figures “don’t tell all of the story.”

A Kansas exit poll he cited ranked cost of living, energy, and groceries as voters’ top issue, at 30.6%.

Cruz called the economy “K-shaped,” with a “yawning divide” between the world’s first trillionaire and millions of families struggling to put food on the table.

Elon Musk became the first person worth $1 trillion in June after Space Exploration Technologies Corp. (NASDAQ:SPCX) strong market debut, and has dipped below and returned to that mark a few times since. On Tuesday, his net worth was at $898 billion, per Bloomberg.

Read Also: Qualcomm, AppLovin, MercadoLibre, Snap and Coherent: Why These 5 Stocks Are on Investors' Radars Today

Tariffs and the Iran War Hit Prices

Tariffs “have made everything too expensive,” Cruz said, and the Iran war “has dragged on too long.”

The war has cost the U.S. military more than $47 billion, per Pentagon data Reuters obtained last month, over 25% above the $37.5 billion Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth cited in July.

The Congressional Budget Office estimated that higher energy prices from the conflict added 2.3 percentage points to annualized inflation in the second quarter.

Cruz said 10.1% of voters named the cost of the Iran war as their top issue and 7.6% named the ongoing Canada trade war.

Warns of a Recession if Investment Stops

“Over $700 billion in new projects are scheduled to start in the next year,” Cruz said.

Should Democrats shut them all down, Cruz predicted, the country would “very likely go into a recession.”

In Texas, Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa, who beat Republican Gov. Greg Abbott, has called for a moratorium on new data centers until lawmakers put real protections in place.

Cruz warned that Texas will become “more like California” if Democrats succeed in “halting all new investment into AI,” while conceding that electricity bills have risen 30% in five years as data centers turned billionaires into “centibillionaires.”

The Dow Jones Industrial Average index posted its strongest post-midterm rally in 44 years and its strongest single-day session in 19 months on Wednesday, jumping 1,569.40 points after Democrats won control of both chambers of Congress, while President Donald Trump celebrated the broader market rally.

According to Ed Yardeni of Yardeni Research, this was Dow’s “strongest post-midterm rally since 1982.”

Fundstrat Global Advisors co-founder and head of research Tom Lee told CNBC the reaction was "healthy" and "kind of expected," saying the election result could force Washington to negotiate.

Lee also said the outcome might "take pressure off the Fed," allowing policymakers to operate more independently, which he said was another reason markets could "rally pretty strongly."

Big Tech’s era of mega buybacks is giving way to an era of mega artificial intelligence spending, as companies put their cash into data centers and technology buildout.

Buybacks Fall to Lowest Level Since 2017

Combined share repurchases by Alphabet Inc. (NASDAQ:GOOGL) (NASDAQ:GOOG), Amazon.com, Inc. (NASDAQ:AMZN), Microsoft Corp. (NASDAQ:MSFT), Meta Platforms Inc. (NASDAQ:META) and Oracle Corp. (NYSE:ORCL) fell to $4.4 billion in the quarter ended in September, the lowest since 2017, The Kobeissi Letter said on X.

That is down about 90% from a peak of roughly $45.9 billion in late 2021, and the third straight quarter below $5 billion.

“AI spending is coming at the expense of Big Tech buybacks,” the market commentator added.

Read Also: TSLA, SPCX Stocks Fall Overnight as Ted Cruz Says Democrats Will ‘Persecute’ Elon Musk: Ron DeSantis Warns ‘I Guarantee You They Will Do That’

MSFT Is the Lone Big Buyer

Microsoft accounted for all of it. The company cut its buybacks to $4.4 billion in the September quarter from $5.7 billion a year earlier.

Alphabet and Meta have sat out the market all year, a sharp reversal from last year, when the two bought back $66.5 billion of their own shares through the first nine months.

Amazon hasn’t repurchased stock since 2022.

Capex Climbs as Borrowing Rises

Alphabet, Meta, Amazon and Oracle are now spending more on data centers and equipment than their operations bring in, while Microsoft is still generating cash.

Alphabet’s capital spending has more than doubled to $51.36 billion in the third quarter from $24 billion a year earlier, while operating cash flow slipped to $42.29 billion from $48.4 billion. Amazon spent $77.26 billion in the quarter, up from $35.1 billion, and expects about $220 billion of cash capital spending for 2026.

Meta narrowed its 2026 capex outlook to $135 billion to $145 billion.

To cover the gap, the companies are borrowing and selling stock. Alphabet’s long-term debt has nearly tripled to $125.10 billion since the end of 2025, and earlier this month Oracle said it would raise $20 billion in debt and equity.

This comes as more than $2 trillion was wiped from the Nasdaq-100’s value in October as scrutiny of AI spending intensified.

Yorkville Ives Partner and tech bull Dan Ives has predicted a 10%-12% downside for chip stocks during the current technology selloff, while Fundstrat’s Tom Lee called the post-election pressure on AI-related names an "overreaction" and said technology stocks could rally 20% from current levels.

Ives Sees More Pain For Chip Stocks

Ives told Bloomberg that investor anxiety has reached a "gut check period" for the technology trade.

According to Ives, hyperscaler capital spending and Palantir Technologies Inc.’s (NASDAQ:PLTR) AI use cases remain supportive, but he sees disruption across memory players, Intel Corp. (NASDAQ:INTC), advertising and software stocks.

Asked how much further chip stocks could fall after the interviewer noted they were roughly 30% below their highs, Ives said, "I think another 10 to 12% down."

He repeated the 10%-12% estimate while discussing the NYSE Semiconductor Index, tracked by iShares Semiconductor ETF (NASDAQ:SOXX), before suggesting that level could begin presenting opportunities to reconsider the sector.

However, Ives said he believes the underlying AI fundamentals will ultimately "prove it out," citing Palantir, Apple Inc. (NASDAQ:AAPL) and the hyperscalers.

Lee Calls AI Selloff An ‘Overreaction’

Lee, Fundstrat Global Advisors’ co-founder and head of research, took a more bullish view following the election-driven pressure on AI and data-center stocks.

"I think there’s a knee-jerk reaction," Lee told CNBC, arguing that rising AI usage would eventually make computing capacity scarce again.

Lee said the "AI trade is very much alive" and argued that states would continue seeking the investment and revenues generated by data-center projects.

"I do think it’s an overreaction today," Lee said. Looking toward year-end, Lee said hedge funds could move back into technology following the correction. "I think a lot of this is going to be a very, very strong tech rally," he added. "Tech could rally 20% from here."

Fundstrat separately said on Wednesday that it viewed the risk-reward for AI and technology as attractive following the midterms.

Arm Holdings PLC (NASDAQ:ARM) CEO Rene Haas acknowledged that rival Advanced Micro Devices Inc. (NASDAQ:AMD) has a long lead in data center chips, but said the company is serious about competing with its first chip.

Faces a Supply Test Against AMD

On Arm’s fiscal second-quarter call Wednesday, Bank of America analyst Vivek Ayyar asked Haas whether Arm has the scale to secure chip supply against AMD.

“AMD has been at it for a long time,” Haas said, pointing to its range of chips and the capacity it buys from Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. “This is our first product.”

Haas said Arm has worked with TSMC, Micron Technology Inc., Samsung Electronics Co., and SK Hynix Inc. for decades, sharing its long-term plans with them, but warned that industry supply will be tight.

“It’s a five to ten year endeavor that’s going to require relationships across all the supply chain. And we’re very, very serious about making sure we get all that done,” he added.

Haas said demand for the Arm AGI CPU, the data center chip Arm launched in March, has strengthened since.

The company has purchase orders from multiple customers that run through calendar 2027, and its first commercial deliveries remain on track for the fiscal fourth quarter.

Arm now expects up to $2 billion in AGI CPU revenue across fiscal 2027 and 2028, up from the more than $1 billion it cited last quarter.

Haas called Meta Platforms Inc. the “chief customer” and said Oracle Corp. plans to offer AGI CPU instances in 2027.

Arm reported second-quarter earnings of 52 cents per share, which beat the analyst estimate of 42 cents, per Benzinga Pro data. Revenue rose 27% year over year to $1.44 billion, ahead of the $1.38 billion estimate.

Microsoft Corp. (NASDAQ:MSFT) spent $5 billion less than expected on AI infrastructure last quarter, with satellite analysis reportedly pointing to construction and permitting delays at two third-party data center projects.

Microsoft disclosed the shortfall during its quarterly earnings call last month. CFO Amy Hood attributed the gap to delays involving outside cloud providers,  without identifying them.

Research firm Aterio identified projects connected to IREN Ltd. (NASDAQ:IREN) as a possible contributor. In Texas, IREN is developing four data centers under a $9.7 billion Microsoft agreement. Aterio’s Oct. 21 satellite review found the Horizon 4 facility without backup generators and cooling equipment, raising questions about its planned year-end delivery.

Aterio captured optical and thermal images of IREN’s Childress campus on Oct. 21 and compared them with satellite imagery from May, June and July to assess construction progress and potential implications for delivery timelines.

IREN previously said equipment shortages delayed Horizon 1, which Microsoft accepted in August, Business Insider reported.

Meanwhile, in New Jersey, DataOne is reportedly developing a Nebius Group N.V. (NASDAQ:NBIS) project under a separate $17.4 billion Microsoft agreement. Aterio analyst Daud Shiraz told Business Insider that about 140 megawatts from the project could move into 2027 after generator-permit problems and additional fuel-cell approval delays. Regulators also fined DataOne $1 million in September.

Notably, Microsoft also scrapped its planned 50-megawatt U.K. data center deal with Nscale in October, due to power supply uncertainty, with grid access reportedly delayed until the 2030s. The site was expected to house 23,000 Nvidia Corp. (NASDAQ:NVDA) GB300 chips.

Microsoft, IREN and Nebius did not immediately respond to Benzinga’s request for comments.

Read Also: AMD's AI Data Center Guarantees Reach $8.5 Billion as It Challenges Nvidia

AI Data Center Buildout Faces New Risks

Microsoft and Alphabet Inc. (NASDAQ:GOOGL) (NASDAQ:GOOG) reported quarterly capital spending below analyst expectations, with Microsoft posting $45.2 billion versus $50.7 billion expected and Alphabet spending $51.36 billion against $55.09 billion. The shortfalls have raised concerns about whether hyperscalers can sustain AI infrastructure spending, potentially affecting demand for neocloud providers.

On Wednesday, technology analyst Dan Ives said that political changes after the Democratic midterm wins could slow the U.S. data center buildout, estimating 10% of planned construction would not proceed.

Qualcomm Inc. (NASDAQ:QCOM) stock fell more than 9% in Thursday’s premarket trading as investors pulled back from semiconductor and artificial intelligence stocks despite the company’s better-than-expected quarterly results.

Nasdaq futures declined 0.53%, while S&P 500 futures gained 0.15%.

Qualcomm stock closed more than 5% higher Wednesday before reversing course in Thursday’s premarket trading.

Qualcomm Beats Earnings Estimates As Automotive Revenue Surges

Qualcomm reported fourth-quarter fiscal 2026 revenue of $10.322 billion, beating Wall Street’s estimate of $10.111 billion. However, revenue declined 8% year over year.

Adjusted earnings of $2.17 per share topped analysts’ estimate of $2.16.

QCT revenue reached $9.015 billion. Handset revenue fell 26% to $5.137 billion, while automotive revenue surged 89% to $1.99 billion. Internet of Things revenue rose 4% to $1.888 billion.

CEO Cristiano Amon highlighted Qualcomm’s first automotive quarter approaching $2 billion. Combined automotive and IoT revenue increased 36% year over year.

Qualcomm Forecasts Strong Data Center Growth

For the first quarter of fiscal 2027, Qualcomm expects revenue of $10.4 billion to $11.2 billion, compared with analysts’ estimate of $10.48 billion.

The company forecasts adjusted earnings of $2.15 to $2.35 per share, compared with the $2.27 consensus.

Qualcomm expects QCT revenue of $9 billion to $9.6 billion and QTL revenue of $1.3 billion to $1.5 billion.

Amon expects non-handset revenue to grow more than 60% in fiscal 2027, supported by automotive, IoT and data centers.

The company expects data-center revenue to exceed $650 million in the December quarter and reach $5 billion for fiscal 2027.

Qualcomm also targets a roughly $7 billion annualized data-center revenue run rate by the end of fiscal 2027 and $15 billion in annual revenue by fiscal 2029.

Qualcomm’s multigenerational agreement with Amazon.com, Inc.’s (NASDAQ:AMZN) Amazon Web Services covers custom AI chips and optical connectivity, with potential purchases of up to $60 billion over 10 years.

Qualcomm is also working with Meta Platforms Inc. (NASDAQ:META) on its Dragonfly C1000 CPU.

Management expects two hyperscaler customers to generate most of its fiscal 2027 data-center revenue.

Automotive, AI And SpaceX Partnerships Drive Expansion

Qualcomm ended fiscal 2026 with automotive revenue running at an annualized $8 billion, exceeding its previous $7 billion expectation.

The company expects growing demand for agentic AI to increase computing requirements across smartphones, smart glasses and robotics.

Qualcomm also signed a multiyear agreement with Space Exploration Technologies Corp. (NASDAQ:SPCX) to support Starlink Mobile’s nationwide terrestrial 5G network.

Smartphone Weakness And Higher Costs Pressure Outlook

Qualcomm expects the global smartphone market to remain flat to slightly lower in calendar 2027 after a low- to mid-teens decline in 2026.

The continued decline in Apple modem-related revenue also remains a challenge. However, management expects automotive, IoT and data-center growth to offset the weakness.

CFO and COO Akash Palkhiwala said fourth-quarter QCT operating margin reached 24%, while QTL’s pretax margin stood at 70%.

Qualcomm returned $2 billion to shareholders through dividends and share repurchases.

The company is raising product prices to offset higher semiconductor costs. It expects the full benefit to reach QCT gross margins in the second half of fiscal 2027.

Investors looking to reduce their exposure to artificial intelligence (AI) may need to rethink their pension exposure. According to an Equable Institute analysis released Wednesday, state and local pension funds hold a lower-bound estimate of $578.1 billion to $706.6 billion in AI-related companies.

Meanwhile, a Wall Street Journal report found that across 13 major public funds, a basket of domestic AI-linked stocks drove $138 billion in paper gains between the end of 2022 and June.

Those gains helped pensions climb out of the hole from the 2008 financial crisis – yet heavily exposed them to one sector with 3 risks building at once: heavy concentration, political backlash against data centers, and warnings of “bubble-like” financing.

A Handful of Giants

As of June 30, 2026, AI-related companies made up 35.1% of all reported public equity investments by state and local pension funds. For funds reporting in the second quarter, the expanded AI basket reached 38.5% of public equity holdings.

The Magnificent 7 account for 63.3% of public AI-related holdings. The largest positions are NVIDIA Corp. at $47.3 billion, Apple Inc. at $42.5 billion, and Microsoft Corp. at $28.2 billion. Funds also reported $4.1 billion in newly listed Space Exploration Technologies Corp. shares.

Overall, at least 9% to 11% of the $6.42 trillion in public pension assets is tied to AI companies. Some funds are far more exposed: Colorado PERA has 18.7% of its total assets in AI, New York City’s pension funds 14.8% and the New York State Teachers’ Retirement System 14.6%.

“A positive economic outcome from the emergence of AI could meaningfully stabilize public pension plans; but a negative event like an AI-bubble bursting could cause very meaningful losses that stakeholders should be aware of,” said Anthony Randazzo, Equable’s executive director.

“Every public pension fund should be doing an internal audit of their own AI exposure and making public the findings.”

See More: Top Momentum Stocks

The Infrastructure Contradiction

The WSJ’s analysis points to a clear contradiction. Pensions rely on AI returns, while local politicians keep fighting the infrastructure AI needs.

In July, New York put a moratorium on many new data center projects while it studies regulation, even as its pension funds’ AI holdings surged. “It’s so contradictory,” said Joseph Hernandez, who ran as the Republican candidate for New York state comptroller. “We’re on both sides of the bet.”

In Pennsylvania and California, officials and union representatives are pushing back over power prices, land use, water consumption and threats to communities.

Sen. Katie Muth [D-PA], who serves on the Public School Employees’ Retirement System board, said many former public employees don’t know their retirements rely partly on AI. She said even she struggles to work out the fund’s exposure: “It’s like being Nancy Drew.”

‘Bubble-Like’ Exuberance

According to David Colla, global head of credit investments at Canada Pension Plan Investment Board (CPPIB), there’s “bubble-like” exuberance in AI financing.

“You cannot wake up one day and just say, ‘Well, we just had this theme that AI was great, and we woke up, and it was 25% of our portfolio,” Colla said for Bloomberg.

Circular financing adds to the risk. Hyperscalers are bankrolling AI upstarts that rely on their products. If smaller players fail, the odds of a domino effect rippling through the ecosystem are significant.

Equable’s $578 billion floor also doesn’t fully capture private equity or corporate debt. Colla said CPPIB is examining off-balance-sheet structures in which shell companies take on the debt needed to build data centers. He said lenders should look even harder at privately held AI developers, whose finances are less transparent.

“There will be winners and losers along the way,” Colla said. “And there’s going to be a lot of volatility.”

Alphabet Inc.‘s (NASDAQ:GOOGL) (NASDAQ:GOOG) Google has created five billionaires. But its biggest wealth-creation story is still concentrated in the hands of the two people who started it: Larry Page and Sergey Brin.

Page and Brin account for more than $513 billion of the $553 billion combined fortune attributed to Alphabet’s billionaire employees, according to a new study.

The remaining three billionaires offer a glimpse of how early equity and careers at a technology giant can also create extraordinary wealth.

Page and Brin Hold 93%

Page has an estimated fortune of $267.4 billion, and Brin, is worth $246.1 billion. Together, they dominate the ranking compiled by trading firm Atmos using Forbes’ real-time billionaire list.

The Google cofounders together hold $513.5 billion, or roughly 93% of the combined wealth attributed to the company’s five billionaires. Alphabet has the largest combined billionaire net worth of any company with at least five billionaire founders or employees in the study.

Google, founded in 1998, has since grown into one of the world’s most valuable technology businesses. Its founders’ fortunes reflect the scale of that expansion — and how much wealth can accrue when founders retain substantial ownership as a company grows.

The Other 3 Billionaires Linked to Alphabet

  • Former CEO Eric Schmidt, who led Google from 2001 to 2011, has an estimated fortune of $36.7 billion.
  • Current CEO Sundar Pichai, who joined the company in 2004, has run Alphabet since 2019.
  • Marissa Mayer, Google’s 20th employee

Read Also: Sundar Pichai Is Using AI Agents to Track Google 24/7

Their inclusion highlights a different side of technology wealth creation. Employees who join a company early or rise into senior leadership can build fortunes that extend far beyond their salaries.

Meta Platforms, Inc. (NASDAQ:META) offers another example. The company has six billionaire employees. The list includes cofounders Mark Zuckerberg, Eduardo Saverin and Dustin Moskovitz and three former staff members. These include Sean Parker, Sheryl Sandberg and infrastructure executive Jeff Rothschild. Their combined wealth stands at $262.9 billion, according to Atmos.

Equity, Not Paychecks

The common thread is ownership. Atmos CEO Nick Cooke said billionaire fortunes are rarely built through salaries, but through shares and stock options accumulated by founders and early employees.

"Billionaires are rarely made with paychecks," Cooke said, noting that employees often accept lower pay early in a company’s life in exchange for equity. As the business expands, those stakes can become enormously valuable.

For investors, Alphabet’s billionaire tally is more than a measure of personal wealth. It illustrates the extraordinary value created by Google’s growth, while underscoring how unevenly that value has been distributed among the people who built the company. Five billionaires may share the distinction, but Page and Brin own almost the entire fortune.

NVIDIA Corp. (NASDAQ:NVDA) stock edged lower in Thursday premarket trading as investors continued rotating away from AI-linked semiconductor stocks following the U.S. midterm elections, even as the broader market held relatively firm.

NVIDIA fell about 0.93% before the bell, while S&P 500 futures rose 0.06%. The Nasdaq-tracking QQQ slipped 0.49%.

Post-Midterm Rotation Pressures Chip Stocks

The weakness extended across the semiconductor group.

Micron Technology Inc. (NASDAQ:MU) fell about 3% in premarket trading after dropping nearly 7% Wednesday, while the iShares PHLX SOX Semiconductor Sector Index Fund (NASDAQ:SOXX) declined almost 3% before the bell following a roughly 3% loss Wednesday.

Tech analyst Dan Ives said semiconductor stocks could fall another 10%-12% during the current pullback.

Fundstrat’s Tom Lee, however, called the AI selloff an "overreaction" and said technology stocks could rally about 20% if hedge funds rotate back into the sector before year-end.

Cramer Sees Tech Leadership Broadening

NVIDIA remains a central AI leader, but CNBC’s Jim Cramer said technology leadership may be expanding beyond the stocks that dominated the market over the past several years.

Cramer said NVIDIA, Microsoft, Alphabet and Meta have struggled to sustain recent rallies, while gains in Broadcom Inc. (NASDAQ:AVGO), Micron, Advanced Micro Devices Inc. (NASDAQ:AMD), Arista Networks Inc. (NYSE:ANET) and Oracle Corp. (NYSE:ORCL) suggest investors may be rotating toward a different group of technology winners.

"Tech’s trying to make a stand here. It’s just not the tech that’s led us for the last few years," Cramer said.

He cautioned against drawing broad conclusions from a single positive trading session.

Data Center Resistance Adds Another Risk

Cramer also pointed to growing resistance to data-center construction over electricity costs and water consumption.

He said smaller developers including IREN Ltd. (NASDAQ:IREN), Nebius Group N.V. (NASDAQ:NBIS) and CoreWeave, Inc. (NASDAQ:CRWV) could face greater exposure to those constraints, while larger companies such as Amazon have more resources and flexibility to shift projects to alternative locations.

The debate comes after semiconductor stocks lost roughly $1 trillion in market value last Friday, as investors questioned whether massive AI infrastructure spending can generate sufficient returns.

Technical Analysis

At $199.40, NVIDIA trades 7.7% below its 20-day SMA of $216.12 and 9.8% below its 50-day SMA of $221.20.

The 20-day SMA has also moved below the 50-day SMA, keeping the intermediate trend under pressure.

NVIDIA is additionally about 2.5% below its 200-day SMA of $204.67, placing the stock below a closely watched long-term trend level.

Earnings And Analyst Outlook

NVIDIA is scheduled to report earnings on Nov. 17, 2026.

Consensus calls for EPS of $2.48, up from $1.30 a year earlier, and revenue of $109.17 billion, compared with $57.01 billion last year.

The stock trades at a 25.3-times P/E multiple.

NVIDIA carries a Buy consensus rating with an average price forecast of $341.04 across 50 analysts, with forecasts ranging from $282 to $515.

Recent actions include Melius Research maintaining Buy while lowering its forecast to $315, Needham maintaining Buy with a $300 forecast and Cantor Fitzgerald maintaining Overweight with a $350 forecast.

A Carson Investment Research strategist stated that the midterm elections resulted in a “blue tsunami” that signals the “beginning of the end” of the Trump era, adding that the shift toward a divided government is “good for markets.”

The ‘Blue Tsunami’

Barry Gilbert, VP, Asset Allocation Strategist at Carson Investment Research, wrote in a Nov. 4 newsletter that Americans have “resoundingly rejected how President Trump has governed in the first two years of his second term.”

Gilbert described the election results as a “blue tsunami,” noting that Democrats are projected to secure a 56-44 majority in the Senate and a 259-176 majority in the House.

Due to this legislative shift, Gilbert stated that Congress will be less cooperative and will try to “thwart his agenda through greater oversight.” However, Gilbert wrote that Trump is “still president,” granting him broad scope on foreign policy, tariffs, and executive orders.

Gilbert highlighted that Trump has averaged 166 executive orders per year in his second term, which Gilbert noted is “a faster pace than any president since FDR.”

Read Also: Dan Ives Warns Chip Stocks Aren't Done Falling, Sees Another 12% Drop — But Tom Lee Calls AI Selloff an 'Overreaction,' Predicts 20% Tech Rally

Market Reaction and Spending

Despite the political realignment, Gilbert noted that the results are positive for equities. “Divided government isn’t likely to slow down the spend, and in the near term that’s good for markets,” Gilbert wrote.

Gilbert observed that Nasdaq futures were initially down near 2% overnight but rose over 2% by morning. According to Gilbert, “Markets are largely indifferent to the federal government’s party configuration.”

‘Beginning of the End’

Gilbert described this period as the “beginning of the end,” explicitly referring to Trump as a “lame duck president” in his final two years. Despite this status, Gilbert cautioned that Trump “is not one to fade into the background.”

Additionally, Gilbert stated that Democrats succeeded because voters viewed them as the “best option to control inflation, focus on American prosperity, and strengthen the middle class.” Gilbert cautioned that if Democrats forget this lesson, “the political gains won’t last long.”

How Has the Stock Market Performed?

The S&P 500 index has advanced 10.36% year-to-date. Similarly, the Nasdaq Composite index was up 9.19%, and the Dow Jones gained 7.04% YTD.

On Wednesday, the SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust (NYSE:SPY) and Invesco QQQ Trust ETF (NASDAQ:QQQ), which track the S&P 500 and Nasdaq-100, respectively, closed higher. SPY rose 1.65% to $766.81, while QQQ advanced 0.97% to $691.95. Meanwhile, the Dow tracker, State Street SPDR Dow Jones Industrial Average ETF Trust (NYSE:DIA), ended 3.10% higher at $533.11.

In premarket trading on Thursday, SPY was up 0.10%, QQQ declined 0.78%, and DIA rose 0.70%.
